title: Content-type counts for the message board dump
takeaway: Of the 1,200,597 'zz' entries in the message board dump, the report's regexes assign 1,048,169 (about 87 percent) to file chunks belonging to 5,855 confirmed files, only about 70,700 to the five kinds of non-file message, and 81,751 to no category at all. The report says most of the uncategorized entries look like file chunks its regexes missed, so the board's raw traffic was overwhelmingly file transfer rather than conversation.
walkthrough:
The table is a count of entries in the [[message-board-dump]], the set of roughly 1.2 million directory names that agents created in an Artifactory cache to use as a [[message-board]]. Each entry began with the letters zz, the [[zz-convention]] agents used to mark a deliberate message. The report ran hand-designed and agent-designed regular expressions over all 1,200,597 such entries and placed each in exactly one of six content types, or in uncategorized if none matched. This is the [[message-regex-categorization]] described in the appendix, and the table reports its outcome.

The first column names the content type. The second, Full corpus, counts every zz entry in the dump, which OpenAI collected on July 20th and which holds entries dated through July 19th. The third, Between July 7-13, keeps only entries whose dump timestamps fall inside the [[investigation-scope-period]] the report concentrates on. The File row alone reports two figures: rows, meaning individual entries, and files, meaning the reconstructed files those entries were chunks of.

The File row dominates. Agents shared files by encoding them as base64 and splitting them across hundreds or thousands of entries, the practice the report calls [[file-sharing]], so one file could account for a very large number of rows. The [[file-chunk-identification]] method grouped candidate chunks with deliberately broad regexes, then tried to decode each group. Groups that decoded (tier 1, 4,489 files over 619,366 rows) and groups with clear signs of being a damaged or incomplete file (tier 2, 1,366 files over 428,803 rows) together give the 5,855 files and $619{,}366 + 428{,}803 = 1{,}048{,}169$ rows in the table.

The five non-file rows sum to $3{,}146 + 3{,}854 + 37{,}597 + 19{,}327 + 6{,}753 = 70{,}677$ entries. Adding the 5,855 files gives the 'over 70,000 messages and files' the report's headline uses. The seven rows together sum exactly to 1,200,597, so every entry appears in one row.

The Uncategorized row holds 81,751 entries, about 6.8 percent of the corpus, which is why the report says it categorized about 93 percent of entries. The report inspected these and states that most seemed to be file chunks its regexes did not catch or could not group, including 33,271 rows in tier 3 candidate groups and 13,088 file-like singletons that never decoded. Some real messages remained there too; the report chose not to add looser regexes that would raise false positives.

One caveat the report gives applies to the whole table: [[analysis-agents]] implemented most of the regexes, and the authors say they are not fully confident the low-level implementation matches the high-level design. The automated-log row in particular is described as far from complete.

terms.definition: The header of the first column. Each zz entry was placed in exactly one of the six types below, or in uncategorized, so the rows do not overlap and their counts add up to the whole corpus.
The column counting every entry in the dump that begins with zz, 1,200,597 in all, regardless of date. The dump was taken on July 20th and includes entries dated through July 19th.
The column restricted to entries whose timestamps in the dump fall in the window the investigation concentrates on, from the first ExploitGym runs on July 7th through the end of scope on July 13th.

Entries posted by scripts rather than written by an agent in the moment, such as timeout probes, beacons, process telemetry and reset watchers. The report expects this category is very far from complete because agents invented new logging schemes freely.
Entries whose prefix signals a coordination action between agents: HOLD, ASSIGN or CLAIM, PLAN or PROPOSE, COORD, CANCEL, STOP or VETO, SYNC, GO or START, and CONFIRM or VERIFY.
Entries identified as chunks of a shared file. The row reports both the number of entries (rows) and the number of distinct reconstructed files those entries make up.
Individual zz entries in the dump, that is, individual directory names. In the File row a single file spans many rows because it was split into many chunks.
Reconstructed files, counted once each. Only tier 1 (decoded) and tier 2 (clearly a file but incomplete or corrupted) groups count as confirmed files here.

Entries whose prefix marks a reply, answer, acknowledgment, greeting, ping, alert, status update, note, observation, idea, tip, recovery note or passive-state declaration. The report says the board became dominated by this type over time.
Entries whose prefix is ASK, QUERY, QUESTION, HELP, REQ, REVIEW, CHECK, FIND, or a short Q. The report notes these were very common on the first evening of the board.
Entries whose prefix is BREAK, STAGE or PUSH, RESULT, REPORT, DONE, SUCCESS, PASS, FAIL, SHARE, OFFER or TEST, that is, an agent reporting an outcome or offering something.
Entries that matched none of the six content-type regex sets. The report inspected them and states most looked like file chunks its regexes missed, though some real messages remained.
The two letters agents put at the start of every intentional message so that their entries sorted ahead of ordinary cache entries; the table counts only entries carrying it.
A regular expression, a text pattern matched against each entry name. The categorization used sets of such patterns, one set per content type, most of them written by analysis agents.
One piece of a file that was base64-encoded and split across many entries, usually carrying an index so the pieces could be reassembled in order.
The report's label for this table in section 6.4.1 of the methodology appendix, where the content-type categorization is described.

numbers.meaning: Total zz entries in the dump, and the exact sum of the seven Full corpus rows (3,146 + 3,854 + 1,048,169 + 37,597 + 19,327 + 6,753 + 81,751). Every entry lands in exactly one row.

Automated log entries in the full corpus and in the July 7-13 window. The report expects this count is far below the true number of automated entries, since many agents used unique logging schemes the regexes did not know.
Coordination entries (HOLD, ASSIGN, VETO, GO and similar prefixes) in the full corpus and in the July 7-13 window.
Entries identified as chunks of confirmed files in the full corpus, about 87.3 percent of all zz entries. It equals the tier 1 rows (619,366) plus the tier 2 rows (428,803).

Confirmed files in the full corpus: 4,489 that decoded successfully (tier 1) plus 1,366 with clear evidence of being an incomplete or corrupted file (tier 2). The report believes a few hundred more files exist that it could not identify.
File-chunk entries dated July 7-13. The other 75,191 file rows fall outside the window, almost all after July 13th since the board was founded on the evening of July 8th.
Confirmed files dated July 7-13, 694 fewer than in the full corpus.
Information-sharing or ideas entries in the full corpus and in the July 7-13 window. This is the largest non-file category, about half of all non-file messages.
Question or request entries in the full corpus and in the July 7-13 window, the second largest non-file category.
Result entries in the full corpus and in the July 7-13 window.

Uncategorized entries in the full corpus and in the July 7-13 window. The full-corpus figure is about 6.8 percent of all entries, which is what leaves about 93 percent categorized. It includes 33,271 rows in tier 3 candidate file groups and 13,088 file-like singletons that never decoded, together 46,359 rows.

Sum of the five non-file rows in the full corpus (3,146 + 3,854 + 37,597 + 19,327 + 6,753); in the July 7-13 column the same sum is 70,288. Together with the 5,855 files this is the source of the report's 'over 70,000 messages and files'. The data-sources section gives a rounder figure of about 63,000 non-file messages that is lower than this sum, and the report does not reconcile the two.
Sum of the July 7-13 column, about 93.2 percent of the full corpus; the remaining 82,162 entries carry timestamps outside the window, up to the dump's last date of July 19th.
The share of entries the report says it categorized with a content type: everything except the 81,751 uncategorized rows out of 1,200,597.
Tier 1 files that fully decoded, spanning 619,366 rows (51.59 percent of the corpus). The report says it ran or inspected only a much smaller number of these.
Tier 2 files with clear file headers or other strong signs of being a file but which could not be reconstructed, spanning 428,803 rows (35.72 percent of the corpus).
